content.title: Thanks for your reviews!
content.comment: We would like to thank all reviewers' careful reviews. And we are glad to see that most of them saw the novelty of the contribution of this paper. Nevertheless, reviewers also pointed out that the writing can be improved and the empirical part needs to be strengthened. In retrospect, we also agree with them on these two points. Improving these two points seem to be not a small modification to the current version of the paper. We, therefore, decide to withdraw this submission. Thanks again for your reviews!

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper introduces a new objective for option discovery that combines expected reward loss with the number of options that the agent needs to consider to solve the task in each episode. The contribution to developing a new algorithm is twofold: firstly, the authors generalized this‘ faster planning objective (from Harb et al.(2018)[1]) for multi-task settings, and secondly, the author developed a setting where only a state-dependent subset of all options is considered in each state. The author demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm in the tabular setting of a four-room environment.

[1] Harb et al, When waiting is not an option: Learning options with a deliberation cost. 2018
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

* The explored idea to use options to achieve faster planning seems very interesting and legit to me;
* The author derives a method to optimize interest functions.

Weaknesses

* The novelty of the new loss seems limited to me as it is a generalization of Harb et al.(2018) [1] to multi-task settings. The proposed interest functions are an interesting contribution but not a crucial one. 
* The experimental part also seems limited as the authors explore the method only in one environment. The straightforward way to strengthen the paper is to consider more environments. 
* There is no comparison with some baselines that use options. I believe the comparison with these baselines in terms of performance and planning metrics (the number of considered options in one episode) will benefit the paper. 
* I miss some qualitative analysis of how interest functions behave, e.g. what kind of options they prioritize for different states. 

Minor issues and questions

* Fig.3(b) shows that MAOC shows that the method has a high variance and only a few launches (sids) achieve the best performance. Am I right?
* In my opinion, it is not easy to see that in Fig.5 FPOC is indeed better than MAOC. Maybe it is better to make this comparison using a histogram or by comparing some statistics (e.g. mean +- std).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The novelty seems limited to me. Some key experiments are missing. I believe the results are reproducible based on the paper details and thanks to the code.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I believe the basic idea of the paper is very interesting, but the novelty of the paper is limited and some key experiments are missing.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes a techniques for discovering options to improve planning efficiency. The technique involves solving a number of tasks, from which the options are learned, and only then do they become available for usage; so it is tailored to the multi-task setting.
The proposed objective is to learn not only to maximize the expected return, but also to minimize the expected number of options that the agents needs to consider in doing so.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper proposes a well formulated objective that has a nice intuitive interpretations.
- The results show that the learned options are intuitively meaningful in the context of the given problem.
- It is interesting to see that it is also possible to learn an interested function and not a pre-defined initiation set for each option.


Weakness:

- How many options are being learned? And how do you define the number of options? Is it pre-defined, or is it implicit in the objective? It would be nice to make this more explicit.

The experimental results are the main drawback in my opinion: 

- The main argument for options is that they allow an agents to learn how to solve tasks quicker. However, the evaluation in the experiments is over the objective J, which is not the original objective of the problem. In such a case, it is difficult to differentiate which term of the objective is the one leading to greater compound returns (J).

- The benchmark for testing options is too simplistic. In my experience, many options methods that seem to work well in toy domains, are very difficult to use in more complex problems. I like the use of toy domains as sanity check and visualization of the learned options, but there should be further testing in different settings.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is well written, but clarity could be improved a bit. I think the authors did a good job at being very precise with notation, but in that precision, there are many subscripts/superscripts that makes it a bit confusing to keep track of what's being discussed.
Especially the difference between \hat{v} and v^{~}

As far as I can tell, the paper is novel, although there is some resemblance to this prior work ( https://arxiv.org/pdf/2001.01577.pdf )

Reproducibility of the method is likely not a major concern, given that the authors provided the code and the description of the method seems to be clear.
content.summary_of_the_review:
A nice paper on option discovery, which also manages to identify useful interest functions.
Unfortunately, the experimental section falls short, as it doesn't highlight practical use cases or test realistic benchmarks against other option discovery techniques.
I would encourage the authors to extends the experiments, to strengthen the overall paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents a hierarchical planning algorithm with focus on designing an objective for discovering options. The objective is centered around composing fewer options per episode and tries to reduce the set of options to consider when making a choice. Experimental results have been provided in the classic two-room and four-room grid-world path planning.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1. The paper is trying to address a very important research problem.
2. Seems like a good solution from as much as I can judge (but the actual algorithms are missing from the main paper so it is hard to assess the correctness of the proposed algorithms).

Improvements:

1. Paper is not self-contained and missing the algorithms which are the major technical contributions of the paper.
2. The experimentation seems to be on a very limited grid-world domain. I would like to see experiments on more complex domains to actually assess the scalability of the algorithm.
3. The work assumes that the exact number of tunable options is known a priori for the domain and this is often not true except for toy grid world domains with a few rooms. The authors do not describe how this limitation can be overcome.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
1. The paper has a lot of spelling and grammar errors and needs significant polishing before publication.
2. The paper also has many technical errors, e.g., (1) Is the caption of Fig 1 correct: "taking the option shown in the figure moves to the three states in the middle with equal probabilities"? It's unclear what three states this is talking about, (2) In the formula on last line of page 7, the h_bar product might require (1 - i(s, h_bar)), etc.
3. The paper's contributions appear to be novel, but I'm unsure about reproducibility since I did not go through the supplementary material and the actual algorithms are deferred to the appendices.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper needs better presentation, polishing and more thorough experimentation. While I believe the paper is making a solid technical contribution, in its current state I cannot recommend acceptance and I will have to give it a weak reject.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose an objective for option learning that is specifically tailored towards faster planning. In their paper, they define faster planning the number of elementary operations needed to achieve a good policy, whatever good may be referring to. The authors focus on the multi-task setting in order to define an objective that would minimize the expected cumulative number of options the agent needs to consider during an episode for each of the SMDP steps. This objective is traded-off with the standard reward maximizing objective through a hyperparameter. The authors also argue for the use of initiation sets to restrict the amount of choices available to the agent. On a tabular domain they show that their objective correlates with lower number of elementary operations, i.e. faster planning.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strengths
- The paper brings the focus on an interesting metric: the speed at which the agent can plan. This is novel to my understanding.
- The paper proposes an intuitive way to achieve this goal
- The authors also show the importance of an interest function

# Weaknesses
- The paper relies on the multi-task setting to discover the options. This can be quite a limitation as we have to assume that tasks are correlated and that a policy can reliably be learned for each of them.
- The paper introduces an important hyperparameter: the one trading \bar{v} and \tilde{v} in equation 2. This hyperparameter is closely related to the deliberation cost and it is well known that the deliberation cost is highly problem-dependent. As the performance of the agent essentially relies on this, it would be necessary to include sensitivity studies on the matter.
- Some parts of the paper a not entirely clear. For example the example in section 3 could be much better presented, it is very important as it is the gateway into the paper.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is not always clear and the notation is a bit confusing. It is not clear to me why we need to introduce option indices. It only seems to obfuscate things even more. 
The paper is of good quality and novelty. However, the presentation of the empirical results doesn't give the full take-away it could. Looking at Figure 3 I am left wondering what exactly were the values of hyperparameters for each of the dots. Also why does Figure 3a consider such an extended period of time? It seems like most of what is interesting already happened at the start.
The authors argue that we need to restrict the number of elementary operations, but by introducing an interest function in order to sample initation sets. Isn't this sampling distribution combinatorial in the number of options? Isn't this problematic from the point of view of computation?
Finally, the work of Khetarpal et al. 2020 is mentioned, but only so slightly. Given how close they are in nature, I would like to see more discussion and more early in the paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes an interesting metric and an proxy objective to maximize it. The evaluation is fair but the presentation of the results could be improved. More ablations would be necessary.

content.title: Toward Discovering Options that Achieve Faster Planning
content.TL;DR: We propose a new objective for option discovery that emphasizes the computational advantage of using options in planning.
content.abstract: We propose a new objective for option discovery that emphasizes the computational advantage of using options in planning. In a sequential machine, the speed of planning is proportional to the number of elementary operations used to achieve a good policy. For episodic tasks, the number of elementary operations depends on the number of options composed by the policy in an episode and the number of options being considered at each decision point. To reduce the amount of computation in planning, for a given set of episodic tasks and a given number of options, our objective prefers options with which it is possible to achieve a high return by composing few options, and also prefers a smaller set of options to choose from at each decision point. We develop an algorithm that optimizes the proposed objective. In a variant of the classic four-room domain, we show that 1) a higher objective value is typically associated with fewer number of elementary planning operations used by the option-value iteration algorithm to obtain a near-optimal value function, 2) our algorithm achieves an objective value that matches it achieved by two human-designed options 3) the amount of computation used by option-value iteration with options discovered by our algorithm matches those with the human-designed options, 4) the options produced by our algorithm also make intuitive sense--they seem to move to and terminate at the entrance of each room.
